candidates.text: Grasso claims the third floor at 9:30 PM, which is when the piano lesson on the floor above was on. Asked about it, Grasso cannot say that the child never did get the passage right — and everybody who was there can.
Found at the suite: A clipping about the failure of Grasso’s business, with Sweeney’s name underlined twice in pencil.
Schilling says Grasso said Sweeney had taken everything and would be made to feel it.
Found at the suite: A promissory note for $4,000 signed by Kreuzer, endorsed to Sweeney, three months past due.
Coffin says Sweeney told Kreuzer that Friday was the end of it, one way or the other.
Found at the third floor: A typed page of dates and sums in Sweeney’s file, headed with Mulcahy’s name.
Schilling says Sweeney told Mulcahy that the story would run whether Mulcahy liked it or not.
Found at the suite: A subpoena naming Sweeney before the grand jury, with Coffin’s name written in the margin.
Hargrove says Sweeney said to Coffin that a man who testifies sleeps better.
Kreuzer hired us, and wants it known that Grasso blamed Sweeney for the ruin of Grasso’s business, and would rather we started there.
Schilling on Kreuzer: Kreuzer’s registration card gives an address on a street that does not exist.
Marchetti on Kreuzer: Two signatures of Kreuzer’s, a month apart, are in different hands.
Hargrove on Kreuzer: Kreuzer answers to the name a half-second late, every time.
A union card in Kreuzer’s coat lining carries a different surname and a 1919 date.
A steamship ticket stub among Kreuzer’s things, in the name of a man who died at Belleau Wood.
The name Kreuzer was born with turns up on a desertion warrant from 1918. Kreuzer has been hiding from the Army for eleven years and from nobody else.
The papers are forged and the reason is plain: Kreuzer was put out of the country once already and does not mean to be put out twice.
Marchetti on Hanrahan: Hanrahan had a key to the third floor that Hanrahan had no business having.
Hargrove on Hanrahan: The accounts at the third floor are in two hands, and the second hand only appears in the last column.
Mulcahy on Hanrahan: Somebody heard a drawer being worked at the third floor some time after 10:00 PM.
A carbon of a deposit slip at the third floor, made out in Hanrahan’s hand to an account in another name.
Ledger pages at the third floor where the totals have been rubbed and written over.
The bank confirms the account: Hanrahan has been taking two hundred a month for a year, and was at the third floor doing exactly that from 10:00 PM. It is theft, and it is not murder.
The books at the third floor settle it. Hanrahan spent from 10:00 PM covering a hole in the accounts, which is why Hanrahan would rather be suspected of anything else.
Grasso on Mulcahy: Mulcahy and Sweeney were heard at the Wyckoff, and one of them was doing all the talking.
Hanrahan on Mulcahy: Mulcahy has come into money lately and has no visible way of having come into money.
Callahan on Mulcahy: Sweeney had been drawing cash in amounts that did not match anything in the accounts.
An envelope at the Wyckoff with nothing in it, addressed in Sweeney’s hand to no one.
A photograph at the Wyckoff, folded small, of something Sweeney would have paid to keep folded.
Sweeney’s bank book settles it: four payments, and Mulcahy at the Wyckoff from 8:00 PM collecting the fifth. It is extortion, and an extortionist wants Sweeney alive.
The thing Mulcahy was holding over Sweeney turns up, and it was worth more to Mulcahy every month than once.
Hargrove on Coffin: Coffin was carrying a parcel into the speakeasy and came out without it.
Kreuzer on Coffin: There is a man who meets people at the speakeasy and nobody will say his name out loud.
Schilling on Coffin: Coffin has been selling things that were never Coffin’s to sell.
Wrapping paper and a cut string at the speakeasy, and the shop it came from closed two years ago.
A pawn ticket at the speakeasy in a name that does not exist, made out at the hour in question.
The receiver at the speakeasy would rather talk than be held: Coffin was there from 8:00 PM handing over a parcel of somebody else’s silver, which is a charge Coffin will take over this one.
The goods turn up, tagged and dated, and the tag puts Coffin at the speakeasy from 8:00 PM with both hands full.
